abstracts.abstract: We introduce a novel framework for solving dynamic graph connectivity problems that fundamentally reconsiders the traditional amortized analysis paradigm. Unlike conventional approaches that maintain forest representations, our method introduces a hierarchical clustering structure with lazy propagation, enabling a completely different amortized cost model. The core innovation lies in treating connectivity queries as operations on a hierarchical partition rather than explicit tree maintenance. We prove that this paradigm shift yields an amortized complexity of O(log n) per operation, matching existing bounds while providing a structurally simpler analysis. More significantly, the new framework naturally extends to fully dynamic weighted graphs where edge weights change over time, a setting where previous approaches require substantial modifications. We establish that our method achieves O(log² n) amortized time for weight updates while maintaining O(log n / log log n) query time, improving upon previously known tradeoffs. The theoretical contribution lies not merely in the specific bounds but in demonstrating that the hierarchical perspective offers a more natural fit for dynamic connectivity problems, potentially influencing future algorithm design in this fundamental domain.

We present a deterministic algorithm for the maximum flow problem in undirected graphs with unit capacities that achieves O(n^{5/3}) time, improving upon the long-standing O(n^{3/2}) bound for this specific case. Our algorithm combines recent advances in expander decomposition techniques with a refined potential function analysis. The key insight is that unit capacity graphs admit a more aggressive use of augmenting paths within the decomposition framework, allowing us to reduce the number of phases required. Specifically, we show that when capacities are uniform, the residual graph's structure enables a more efficient implementation of blocking flow computations, yielding the improved exponent from 3/2 to 5/3. We also extend our analysis to bipartite matching, obtaining an O(n^{5/3}) algorithm that improves on existing deterministic bounds. The running time analysis is tight up to logarithmic factors for our approach, and we provide lower bounds suggesting that further improvement would require substantially new techniques. This work demonstrates that the recent surge of interest in fine-grained graph algorithms continues to yield practical improvements in fundamental combinatorial optimization problems.

We present CacheTree, a novel cache-oblivious data structure for range reporting queries that fundamentally reconceptualizes the traditional memory hierarchy model. Existing cache-oblivious structures suffer from significant constant factors that render them impractical despite their theoretically optimal I/O complexity. CacheTree addresses this gap by introducing a two-level layout strategy that maintains theoretical optimality while adapting to real-world cache parameters. The first level uses a coarse-grained partition that aligns with typical L2 cache sizes, while the second level provides fine-grained organization for L1 cache optimization. We provide a complete implementation with detailed empirical analysis across diverse hardware platforms. Our experimental results demonstrate that CacheTree achieves performance within 15% of naive cache-aware solutions while maintaining provably optimal cache-oblivious behavior. The design introduces a new paradigm for bridging the theory-practice gap in memory hierarchy optimization, showing that modest structural modifications can yield substantial practical benefits without sacrificing theoretical guarantees.

We present a highly optimized implementation of the Edmonds-Karp algorithm for maximum flow computation that achieves order-of-magnitude speedups over existing library implementations. Our approach combines three complementary optimization strategies: intelligent residual graph representation using hybrid adjacency structures, bottleneck-aware path selection heuristics that maintain theoretical guarantees, and aggressive early termination detection. The hybrid representation dynamically switches between adjacency lists and matrices based on graph density and operation patterns, yielding optimal memory access characteristics across diverse input types. Our bottleneck-aware heuristic identifies and eliminates redundant augmentations without compromising correctness, reducing the number of iterations by an average of 60% on real-world networks. Extensive experiments on graphs from transportation, social, and computational biology domains demonstrate that our implementation outperforms leading libraries including Lemon and NetworkX by factors of 8-25x while maintaining identical output. The implementation is available as open-source software with a clean API, enabling straightforward integration into existing systems.
